property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner and any target newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) sets c.owner() equal to the provided newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender and thus breaks this property when owner != newOwner.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address newOwner != caller, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) makes c.owner() equal to newOwner (the reference assigns the passed newOwner, the mutant assigns msg.sender and thus will differ for some fuzzed newOwner).

For any initial owner and any address newOwner, if the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner getter equals the provided newOwner afterwards; the mutant that assigns msg.sender instead will fail this for cases where newOwner != caller.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address newOwner (possibly equal to caller), after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner getter equals the provided newOwner; the mutant that assigns msg.sender instead will violate this when newOwner != caller.

For any owner caller and any address newOwner, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner getter equals the provided newOwner afterwards; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender breaks this because it sets owner to the caller instead of the provided newOwner for some fuzzed newOwner values.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) updates C.owner() to newOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment breaks this by leaving owner unchanged for some inputs.

For any caller equal to the current owner and any newOwner address (except address(0)), after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() equals newOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment can leave owner() unchanged for some newOwner, violating this rule.

For any caller that is equal to the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds (does not revert) and afterwards the contract's owner() equals newOwner; the mutant that omits the assignment can leave owner() unchanged, violating this property for some fuzzed newOwner.

For any non-zero newOwner and when called by the current owner, transferOwnership succeeds and sets owner() to the provided newOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment will still succeed but leave owner() unchanged for some fuzzed newOwner, violating this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) does not revert and afterwards C.owner() equals the provided newOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment breaks this by leaving owner() unchanged for some fuzzed newOwner values.

For any caller address A and newOwner address N, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(N) the owner becomes N; the mutant inverted the ownership guard so if the current owner calls transferOwnership it will be rejected (or changed only when caller is not current owner), causing owner() to differ for some inputs.

For any caller address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) as the contract's owner should succeed and update c.owner() to newOwner; the mutant's forced revert in the onlyOwner modifier causes the call to always revert, so c.owner() does not become newOwner for some inputs.

Invariant: Only the current owner can call owned() without changing the owner; the reference leaves owner unchanged after any call to owned(), whereas the mutant incorrectly sets owner = msg.sender inside owned(), allowing owner to change upon an owned() call.

Invariant: calling owned() must NOT change the contract's owner — the reference preserves owner across any owned() call by the current owner, while the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() and thus changes owner when owned() is invoked.

For any caller who is already the contract owner, calling owned() must succeed (not revert) and must NOT change the owner; the mutant sets owner = msg.sender inside owned(), causing owner to remain unchanged in the reference but potentially unchanged as well — to make a distinguishing property we instead check that a non-owner cannot call owned() (it reverts) for all addresses, while the mutant may unintentionally allow owner-changing behavior only when the caller is owner; therefore the safe universal property we assert is: only the current owner can successfully call owned() (calls from non-owners always revert) — the mutant preserves the require but changes state for owner calls, so to detect the mutant we fuzz two distinct addresses and check that a non-owner call reverts while the owner call succeeds and does not change who the owner is afterward.

For any two distinct addresses A (current owner) and B (another address), if the contract's owner is set to A then after A calls owned() the owner remains A (reference preserves owner), but the mutant may change owner to A again (no change) — this doesn't distinguish; instead we assert that if owner is A and B calls owned() it MUST revert (non-owners cannot call owned()); the mutant still reverts for non-owners so to distinguish we instead choose to fuzz-initialize owner to some address X via transferOwnership(X) called by the initial owner, then have that owner call owned() and assert owner stays X — the mutant changes owner when owned() is called by the owner only if the owner differs from msg.sender after a prank; to force difference we fuzz two addresses and perform the sequence with pranks so the mutant's state write is observable: the universal rule is that after the current owner calls owned(), the owner remains equal to the caller (i.e., owner is stable when called by the owner), and the mutant breaks this when the initial owner was different from the deployer — we therefore fuzz two addresses (deployer and newOwner) and ensure the sequence captures the mutant's extra assignment.

For every admissible pair of distinct addresses ownerCandidate and caller, if the contract's owner is set to ownerCandidate, then when ownerCandidate (the current owner) calls owned() the owner remains equal to ownerCandidate afterwards; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can break this when the caller is not the canonical owner, so we fuzz two addresses and ensure only the true owner can call owned() successfully and that a successful call by the owner preserves ownership.

General rule: only the contract owner can call owned(), so calling owned() must never change the owner address; the mutant removes the require check allowing non-owners to call owned() and (if owned() changed owner) thereby create caller-dependent owner changes which violate this property.

The owner state variable never changes when owned() is called by any non-owner; the mutant removes the onlyOwner check allowing a non-owner call to owned() to change owner (so for some caller the post-call owner differs).

For all callers, calling owned() does not change C.owner() (only the current owner can perform owner-only state changes); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so some non-owner caller can cause owner() to differ after calling owned().

Invariant: only the current owner can change the owner via transferOwnership; the mutant removing the onlyOwner check allows some other caller to change owner, violating this rule for some fuzzed caller addresses.

For any caller who is the owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership sets c.owner() to the supplied newOwner (including address(0)); the mutant prevents setting owner to address(0) so it violates this for inputs where newOwner == address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always makes c.owner() equal newOwner; the mutant (which forbids newOwner == address(0)) violates this when newOwner == address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner; the mutant (which forbids newOwner == address(0)) violates this rule for inputs where newOwner == address(0) by leaving owner unchanged or reverting.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) will result in c.owner() equaling newOwner for every admissible newOwner (including address(0)); the mutant that rejects address(0) breaks this by preventing/ reverting when newOwner == address(0).

For any admissible pair (caller, newOwner) where caller is the current owner and newOwner is any non-zero or zero address, the reference allows transferring ownership to that newOwner (so after transferOwnership the getter owner() equals newOwner); the mutant forbids newOwner == address(0), so it violates the rule for inputs with newOwner == address(0).
